sections.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Case Triage Routing

content.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Case Triage Routing
content.overview: This section provides a trauma-informed, practical guide to understanding the core purpose of case triage routing and how it shapes physical, emotional, and relational safety in daily family life. Designed for parents, caregivers, and family support practitioners, it focuses on realistic, repeatable steps that strengthen safety, predictability, and connection.
content.psychoeducation: Why does case triage routing matter in section 1? Children and families thrive on predictability, nervous-system safety, and attuned repair. When case triage routing is practised consistently, stress responses decrease and relational trust grows. Triage routing determines workflow attention, not the final outcome of a case
learning_goals: Differentiate low, moderate, high, and critical routing pathways using explicit criteria (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Case Triage Routing)
Match triage outputs to the right tasks, alerts, owners, and response timeframes (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Case Triage Routing)
Recognise when a case needs escalation because of change velocity, not just absolute severity (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Case Triage Routing)
Use human checkpoints to confirm that routing is appropriate before sensitive action proceeds (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Case Triage Routing)
step_by_step: Pause & Ground: Notice your own breathing, body tension, and tone before addressing case triage routing.
Observe Factually: Notice what is happening in the moment around case triage routing without blame or judgement.
Connect & Validate: Acknowledge feelings and safety needs clearly and calmly.
Respond Simply: Choose one clear, age-appropriate action or boundary for case triage routing.
Reflect & Repair: Review what worked, repair any rupture honestly, and record your next small step.
parent_scripts: "I can see this moment feels big right now. Let's slow down and take one step together with case triage routing."
"Everyone is safe here. We can talk about what happened and work out the next step calmly."
"I noticed I was getting stressed. I'm taking a breath so I can listen properly."
"We don't have to get everything perfect today — we are practising case triage routing one routine at a time."
practical_examples: Everyday Routine: Applying case triage routing during a busy morning or bedtime transition by slowing down, offering two calm choices, and keeping tone steady.
Moment of Stress: When tension rises around case triage routing, pausing for 10 seconds before speaking, validating feelings, and focusing on safety first.
Follow-Through & Review: Recording a factual note after practising case triage routing to notice what helped the child settle and what support would help next time.
reflection_questions: What signals tell me a case may need a faster or more senior response?
How do I balance urgency with uncertainty?
Where are routing expectations least clear in my service?
What review step most improves confidence in triage decisions?
practice_ideas: Sort sample cases into routing tiers and explain the threshold used
Map each tier to follow-up tasks, reviewer roles, and expected timeframes
Identify a case where rising risk should change routing even if the absolute score is moderate
Review a misrouted case and describe the operational consequences
content.closing_message: Progress in case triage routing comes from small, consistent moments of safety, honesty, and repair — not perfection. Every time you pause, stay regulated, and choose a safer response, you build lasting trust.

content_variants.toddlers: For babies & toddlers (0–4): Focus on gentle tone, physical comfort, predictable routines, and simple 3-to-5 word reassurance while practising case triage routing.
content_variants.school_age: For school-age children (5–11): Use clear explanations, visual routines, curiosity about their feelings, and collaborative problem-solving around case triage routing.
content_variants.teens: For adolescents (12–18): Respect autonomy, listen without lecturing, agree on clear safety boundaries, and involve teens in decisions about case triage routing.
content_variants.fatherhood: For fathers & male caregivers: Model calm accountability, steady emotional presence, and non-frightening leadership when practising case triage routing.

red_flags: Immediate physical danger, threats, intimidation, or coercive control observed during case triage routing.
A child shows fear, freezing, dissociation, or disclosure of harm related to case triage routing.
An adult is unable to regulate or maintain safe supervision while attempting case triage routing.
Signs of acute mental health crisis or substance intoxication affecting child safety.
when_to_escalate: Pause learning immediately if anyone is in danger and use verified emergency or crisis supports.
Follow jurisdiction-specific child protection and mandatory reporting obligations when harm is disclosed or suspected.
Engage a qualified supervisor, specialist DFV practitioner, or clinician when risk exceeds self-directed learning.

trauma_informed.clinical: Nervous-system lens for case triage routing: Recognises fight, flight, freeze, and fawn survival responses, window of tolerance, and the need for co-regulation before cognitive problem-solving.
trauma_informed.relational: Attachment lens for case triage routing: Prioritises connection before correction, attunement to cues, shame-free accountability, and timely repair after ruptures.
trauma_informed.justice: Fairness & cultural lens for case triage routing: Respects cultural strengths, kinship networks, neurodiversity, disability access, and structural barriers without equating poverty with neglect.
trauma_informed.fatherhood: Accountable fatherhood lens for case triage routing: Replaces control or withdrawal with steady, reliable care, honest repair, and child-centred safety.

sections.simplified_parent_version:
What case triage routing means:
Case Triage Routing is about keeping daily life safe, calm, and predictable so your child feels supported and understood.

How to practise it:
1. Pause and take one slow breath first.
2. Notice what your child needs right now.
3. Use a calm voice and one clear step.
4. Repair kindly if things go off track.

content.overview: This lesson helps practitioners route cases into the right response pathway based on current risk, urgency, complexity, and review requirements. It focuses on consistent triage logic, transparent thresholds, and making sure the safest response is visible to the right people at the right time.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate low, moderate, high, and critical routing pathways using explicit criteria
Match triage outputs to the right tasks, alerts, owners, and response timeframes
Recognise when a case needs escalation because of change velocity, not just absolute severity
Use human checkpoints to confirm that routing is appropriate before sensitive action proceeds
key_concepts: Triage routing determines workflow attention, not the final outcome of a case
Routing should account for urgency, uncertainty, and coordination needs as well as score bands
Visible ownership and timeframes reduce response drift in complex cases
High-risk routing must notify accountable humans rather than automate adverse action
practice_activities: Sort sample cases into routing tiers and explain the threshold used
Map each tier to follow-up tasks, reviewer roles, and expected timeframes
Identify a case where rising risk should change routing even if the absolute score is moderate
Review a misrouted case and describe the operational consequences
facilitator_notes: Frame triage as a prioritisation tool that supports safer coordination
Use examples that show both over-escalation and under-escalation risks
Discuss workload pressure openly so participants can see where triage drift happens
Keep emphasis on notification, review, and response discipline
reflection_prompts: What signals tell me a case may need a faster or more senior response?
How do I balance urgency with uncertainty?
Where are routing expectations least clear in my service?
What review step most improves confidence in triage decisions?
content.printable_summary:
Case Triage Routing — Key Takeaways:
- Route for urgency, complexity, and change, not score alone.
- Tie each tier to owners, tasks, and timeframes.
- Use routing to improve visibility and coordination.
- Confirm sensitive escalations through human checkpoints.
